And once, when it had led Lysimachus to the executioner and he was sitting there already about to die, Eumelides of Alopece took him away, saying that no citizen ought to die without a verdict of a law-court; and when a trial took place in court, Lysimachus was acquitted, and got the nickname "the man from the drum"; and the people took away from the Council the power to put to death and to imprison and to fine, and laid down a law that if the Council should condemn anyone of wrongdoing or impose a fine, the thesmothetae should bring the condemnations and the fines into the law-court, and whatever the jurors should vote, this should be authoritative.

2. The Council tries most of the magistrates, especially those that handle money; but its judgement is not final, but subject to appeal to the law-court. It is permitted also for private persons to lay information against any office they wish for not using the laws; and for these too there is appeal to the law-court, if the Council condemns them.
3. It also scrutinizes the councillors who are to serve the next year, and the nine archons. Formerly it had authority to reject finally, but now there is appeal for these to the law-court.

4. In these matters, then, the Council is not final; but it draws up preliminary resolutions for the people, and it is not permitted for the people to vote on anything not previously resolved on, nor anything that the prytanes have not put on the agenda. For on these very grounds the man who carries a measure is liable to an indictment for illegal proposals.

1. It also takes charge of the triremes already built, and the tackle, and the ship-sheds, and it builds new triremes or quadriremes, whichever the people votes, and tackle for these and ship-sheds; and the people elects master-builders for the ships. If they do not hand these over completed to the new Council, they cannot receive the bounty; for they receive it under the following Council. It builds the triremes, having chosen ten men from among themselves as trireme-builders.
2. It also examines all the public buildings, and if anyone seems to it to be doing wrong, it reports him to the people, and on condemning him hands him over to a law-court.

1. It also helps administer most matters with the other offices. First, the treasurers of Athena are ten, one allotted from each tribe, from the five-hundred-bushel men according to the law of Solon (for the law is still in force), and the man allotted holds office even if he is very poor. They take over the statue of Athena and the Victories and the rest of the adornment and the funds in the presence of the Council.

2. Next the sellers, who are ten, one allotted from each tribe. They let out all the contracts, and sell the mines and the taxes, together with the treasurer of military funds and those chosen for the theoric fund, in the presence of the Council, and they confirm the sale for whomever the Council approves by show of hands, both the mines sold—the workable ones sold for three years, and those granted for working sold for ten—and they sell, in the presence of the Council, the property of those exiled from the Areopagus and of the others, and the nine archons ratify it. The taxes sold for the year they record on whitened tablets, the buyer and the price at which he bought, and hand them over to the Council.

3. They record separately those who must pay in each presidency, on ten tablets, and separately those who pay three times in the year, making a tablet for each payment, and separately those who pay in the ninth presidency. They also record the lands and houses registered and sold in the law-court; for these too these men sell. Of the houses the price must be paid within five years, of the lands within ten; and they pay these in the ninth presidency.

4. The king also brings in the leases of the sacred precincts, recorded on whitened tablets. Of these too the lease is for ten years, and payment is made in the ninth presidency; which is why the most money is collected in this presidency.

5. The tablets recorded according to the payments are brought into the Council, and the public slave keeps them; and whenever there is a payment of money, he takes down these very tablets from the shelves and hands them over to the receivers—those on which the money must be paid and erased on that day; the rest are stored apart, that they may not be erased prematurely.

1. There are ten receivers, allotted by tribes. These, taking the tablets, erase the money that is paid in, in the presence of the Council in the Council-house, and again hand the tablets back to the public slave. And if anyone falls short in a payment, it is recorded there, and he must pay double the amount deficient or be imprisoned; and the Council has authority to exact this and to imprison according to the laws.

2. On the first day, then, they receive all the money and apportion it to the offices; and on the next day they bring in the apportionment, written on a board, and read it out in the Council-house, and put before the Council the question whether anyone knows of any wrongdoing concerning the apportionment, by a magistrate or a private person, and they put proposals to the vote if anyone seems to be doing wrong.
3. The councillors also allot from among themselves ten auditors, who are to audit the offices in each presidency.

4. They also allot one examiner for each tribe, and two assessors for each of the examiners, who must sit in the markets beside the statue of the eponymous hero of each tribe, so that, if anyone wishes, within three days from the day on which a magistrate has rendered his accounts in the law-court, to bring against any of those who have rendered accounts an examination, whether private or public, he writes on a whitened tablet his own name and that of the defendant, and the wrong of which he accuses him, and adding whatever penalty he thinks fit, gives it to the examiner.

5. He, taking it and inquiring into it, if he condemns, hands over the private matters to the deme-judges who try cases for that tribe, and the public ones he records jointly with the thesmothetae. And the thesmothetae, if they take it up, bring this examination again into the law-court, and whatever the jurors decide, this is final.

1. The Council also examines the horses, and if anyone seems to be keeping a good horse badly, it punishes him with the loss of the fodder-allowance; and on those that cannot keep up, or will not stand still but are unruly, it brands a wheel on the jaw, and the horse that has suffered this is rejected. It also examines the scouts, whichever of them seem to it fit to act as scouts, and any whom it rejects by vote has dismounted. It also examines the mounted foot-soldiers, and any whom it rejects by vote ceases to draw pay.

2. The cavalry are enrolled by the enrolling officers, ten men whom the people elects; and whomever they enroll they hand over to the cavalry-commanders and tribal commanders, and these, taking them over, bring the list into the Council, and opening the tablet on which the names of the cavalry are sealed up, they erase those previously enrolled who swear they are not able in body to serve as cavalry, and call up those newly enrolled; and if anyone swears that he is not able in body to serve, or in property, they release him, but the one who does not swear off the councillors vote on, whether he is fit to serve as cavalry or not. And if they vote him fit, they write him in the tablet; if not, they release him too.

3. Formerly the Council also judged the models and the robe, but now the law-court chosen by lot does; for the councillors were thought to show favour in their judgement. And of the making of the Victories and the prizes for the Panathenaea it takes charge jointly with the treasurer of military funds.

4. The Council also examines the disabled; for there is a law that orders those possessing less than three minae and so maimed in body that they cannot do any work, to be examined by the Council, which gives them maintenance at the public expense, two obols a day each. And there is a treasurer for them, chosen by lot.
5. It also helps administer most of the affairs of the other offices, so to speak.

1. These, then, are the matters administered by the Council. Ten men are also allotted as repairers of sacred buildings, who, receiving thirty minae from the receivers, repair the sacred buildings most in need.

2. And ten city-controllers. Of these five hold office in the Piraeus and five in the town, and they oversee the flute-girls and the harp-girls and the lyre-girls, that they shall not be hired for more than two drachmas, and if more than one are eager to take the same girl, these men cast lots and let her out to the one who wins. They take care also that none of the dung-collectors deposits dung within ten stades of the wall. They prevent men from building over the roads, and from extending balconies over the roads, and from making overhead pipes with their outflow into the road, and from opening windows toward the road. And they remove those who die in the roads, having public slaves to do it.

1. Ten market-controllers are also allotted, five for the Piraeus, five for the town. To these it is enjoined by the laws to take charge of all goods for sale, that they may be sold pure and unadulterated.
2. Ten measure-controllers are also allotted, five for the town, five for the Piraeus. And these take charge of all the measures and weights, that the sellers may use just ones.

3. There were also corn-guardians, ten allotted, five for the Piraeus, five for the town, but now twenty for the town and fifteen for the Piraeus. These take care, first, that the unground corn in the market shall be sold justly, then that the millers shall sell barley-meal at prices corresponding to those of the barley, and the bread-sellers their loaves at prices corresponding to those of the wheat, and of the weight that these men fix; for the law orders them to fix it.

4. They allot ten superintendents of the trading-place; to these it is enjoined to take charge of the trading-places, and to compel the merchants to bring up to the town two-thirds of the corn that sails down into the corn-market.

1. They establish also by lot the Eleven, those who are to take charge of those in the prison, and to put to death the thieves, kidnappers, and clothes-stealers who are led off, if they confess, but if they dispute, to bring them into the law-court, and if they are acquitted, to release them, but if not, then to put them to death; and to bring into the law-court the lands and houses registered, and to hand over to the sellers what is decided to be public property, and to bring in the informations; for these too the Eleven bring in. Some of the informations the thesmothetae also bring in.

2. They allot also five introducers, who introduce the monthly suits, each for two tribes. The monthly suits are those concerning dowry, if a man owing it does not pay it, and if a man who has borrowed at the rate of a drachma defrauds, and if a man wishing to do business in the market borrows capital from someone; further, suits of assault, of contributions, of partnership, of slaves, of beasts of burden, of trierarchy, and of banking.

3. These men, then, judge these monthly suits introducing them; but the receivers judge the suits for and against the tax-farmers, having authority up to ten drachmas, and the rest they introduce into the law-court as monthly suits.

1. They allot also the Forty, four from each tribe, before whom men bring the other suits. Formerly they were thirty and went round the demes to try cases, but after the oligarchy of the Thirty they became forty. Cases up to ten drachmas they have authority to decide themselves, but those above this assessment they hand over to the arbitrators.

2. These, taking them over, if they cannot effect a settlement, give a decision; and if the decision pleases both parties and they abide by it, the suit is at an end. But if either of the litigants appeals to the law-court, they place the testimonies and the challenges and the laws in jars—separately those of the prosecutor, separately those of the defendant—and sealing these up, and attaching the arbitrator's decision written on a tablet, they hand them over to the four who try cases for the defendant's tribe.

3. These, taking them over, bring them into the law-court, those under a thousand drachmas before a panel of two hundred and one, those over a thousand before one of four hundred and one. It is not permitted to use either laws or challenges or testimonies except those that the arbitrator has placed in the jars.

4. The arbitrators are those who are in their sixtieth year. This is clear from the archons and the eponymous heroes. For there are ten eponymous heroes of the tribes, and forty-two of the age-classes; and the ephebes, when enrolled, were formerly recorded on whitened tablets, and there were inscribed beside them the archon in whose year they were enrolled, and the eponymous hero who had served as arbitrator in the previous year; but now they are recorded on a bronze pillar, and the pillar stands before the Council-house beside the eponymous heroes.

5. The Forty, taking the last of the eponymous heroes, distribute the arbitrations among them and allot which each shall arbitrate; and each man is obliged to carry through the arbitrations he is allotted. For the law orders that anyone who does not become an arbitrator when his age-class falls due shall be without civic rights, except if he happens to be holding some office in that year, or to be abroad; these alone are exempt.

6. It is permitted also to lay an information against the arbitrators, if anyone is wronged by an arbitrator; and if they condemn anyone, the laws order him to be deprived of civic rights. There is appeal also for these.
7. They use the eponymous heroes also for campaigns, and when they send out an age-class, they announce from which archon and eponymous hero to which they must serve.
1. They allot also the following offices: five road-makers, to whom it is enjoined to repair the roads, having public workmen;

2. and ten auditors and ten advocates for these, to whom all who have held office must render account. For these alone are the ones who audit those subject to account and bring the audits into the law-court. And if they convict anyone of theft, the jurors condemn for theft, and the amount adjudged is repaid tenfold. If they show that anyone has taken bribes and the jurors condemn, they assess for bribery, and this too is repaid tenfold. But if they condemn anyone of wrongdoing, they assess for wrongdoing, and this is repaid singly, if a man pays before the ninth presidency, but if not, it is doubled. The tenfold penalty is not doubled.

3. They allot also the secretary called by the presidency, who is in charge of the documents, and keeps the decrees that are passed, and countersigns everything else and sits beside the Council. Formerly this man was elected, and they used to elect the most distinguished and trustworthy; for on the pillars, beside the alliances and grants of proxeny and citizenship, this man is recorded. But now he has become allotted.
4. They allot also another for the laws, who sits beside the Council and countersigns all the laws too.
5. The people also elects a secretary to read out to it and to the Council, and this man has authority over nothing but the reading.

6. It allots also ten commissioners of sacrifices, those called the commissioners for expiatory offerings, who sacrifice the oracular sacrifices, and, if any favorable omens must be obtained, obtain them with the seers.

7. It allots also another ten, those called the yearly commissioners, who perform certain sacrifices and administer all the quadrennial festivals except the Panathenaea. The quadrennial festivals are: one, that to Delos (there is also a sexennial one there); second, the Brauronia; third, the Heracleia; fourth, the Eleusinia; fifth, the Panathenaea; and none of these falls in the same year. Now there has been added also the Hephaestia, in the archonship of Cephisophon.
8. They allot also an archon for Salamis, and a demarch for the Piraeus, who hold the Dionysia in each place and appoint the producers. In Salamis the name of the archon is also recorded.

1. These offices, then, are allotted and have authority over the matters described. As for the so-called nine archons, the way they were established at first has been told; but now they allot six thesmothetae and a secretary for them, and besides an archon, a king, and a polemarch, by turns from each tribe.

2. These are scrutinized first in the Council of Five Hundred, except the secretary; he is scrutinized only in the law-court, like the other magistrates (for all, both the allotted and the elected, hold office after being scrutinized), but the nine archons both in the Council and again in the law-court. Formerly a man whom the Council rejected did not hold office, but now there is appeal to the law-court, and this is authoritative for the scrutiny.

3. They ask, when they scrutinize, first: "Who is your father, and from what deme, and who is your father's father, and who your mother, and who your mother's father, and from what deme?" After this, whether he has an Apollo Patroös and a Zeus Herceios, and where these sanctuaries are; then whether he has family tombs, and where they are; then whether he treats his parents well, and pays his taxes, and has performed his military service. Having asked these things, "Call," he says, "the witnesses to these matters."

4. When he has provided the witnesses, he asks: "Does anyone wish to accuse this man?" And if there is an accuser, he gives accusation and defence, and so puts it, in the Council, to the show of hands, in the law-court to the vote. But if no one wishes to accuse, he puts it at once to the vote. And formerly one man cast the ballot, but now all must vote on them, so that, if some scoundrel has got rid of his accusers, it may be in the jurors' power to reject him.

5. Having been scrutinized in this way, they go to the stone on which are the pieces of the victims, on which the arbitrators too swear before declaring their decisions, and the witnesses swear off their testimonies. Going up onto this, they swear to rule justly and according to the laws, and not to take gifts on account of their office, and, if they take anything, to dedicate a golden statue. Having sworn from there, they go to the Acropolis and swear the same things again there, and after this they enter upon their office.

1. The archon and the king and the polemarch each take two assessors whom they wish, and these are scrutinized in the law-court before assessing, and render accounts when they have finished assessing.

2. The archon, as soon as he has entered office, first proclaims that whatever anyone held before his entering office, he shall hold and possess until the end of his term. Then he appoints three producers for the tragedies,

3. choosing from all the Athenians the richest; formerly he appointed five for the comedies too, but now the tribes furnish these. Then, taking over the producers furnished by the tribes for the Dionysia—for men, boys, and comedies—and for the Thargelia for men and boys (those for the Dionysia are by tribes, but for the Thargelia one for two tribes, and each tribe furnishes in turn)—he conducts the exchanges of property for these and brings in the exemptions, if anyone says he has performed this service before, or is exempt as having performed another service and the period of his exemption has not run out, or is not of age; for the producer for the boys must be over forty years of age. He appoints producers also for Delos, and a chief delegate for the thirty-oared ship that carries the youths.

4. He takes charge of the processions—that which is held for Asclepius, when the initiates keep house, and that of the Great Dionysia, together with the supervisors, whom formerly the people elected, ten in number, and they paid the expenses of the procession from their own means, but now it allots one from each tribe and gives a hundred minae for the equipment.

5. He takes charge also of the procession at the Thargelia and of that for Zeus the Saviour. He administers also the contest of the Dionysia and of the Thargelia. Of festivals, then, he takes charge of these.

6. Indictments and suits are brought before him, which, after examining, he brings into the law-court: for ill-treatment of parents (these are free from risk for any who wishes to prosecute), for ill-treatment of orphans (these are against the guardians), for ill-treatment of an heiress (these are against the guardians and those who dwell with her), for ill-treatment of an orphan's estate (these too are against the guardians), for insanity, if anyone accuses another of destroying his property in madness, for the choice of dividers, if anyone is unwilling to have common property divided, for the establishment of a guardianship, for the adjudication of a guardianship, for the production of property, for entering oneself as a guardian, and the adjudications of estates and heiresses.

7. He takes charge also of the orphans and the heiresses and the women who, when the husband has died, claim to be pregnant. And he has authority to fine wrongdoers or to bring them into the law-court. He lets out the estates of the orphans and the heiresses until one reaches fourteen years of age, and receives the securities, and from the guardians, if they do not give the children their maintenance, he exacts it.

1. The archon, then, takes charge of these things. The king first takes charge of the Mysteries, together with the supervisors whom the people elects, two from all the Athenians, one from the Eumolpidae, one from the Heralds. Then of the Dionysia at the Lenaeum; these are a procession and a contest. The procession the king and the supervisors send out in common, but the contest the king administers. He holds also all the torch-races; and, so to speak, he administers all the ancestral sacrifices.

2. Indictments for impiety are brought before him, and if anyone disputes a priesthood with another. He adjudicates also for the clans and the priests all the disputes concerning sacred matters. Before him too are brought all the suits of homicide, and it is he who proclaims that a man is excluded from the customary rites.

3. There are suits of homicide and of wounding: if a man kills or wounds with forethought, in the Areopagus; and of poisoning, if he kills by giving it; and of arson; for these alone the Council tries. For the involuntary, and for planning, and if anyone kills a slave or a metic or a foreigner, the court at the Palladion. If a man admits the killing but says it was according to the laws—for instance, having caught an adulterer, or in ignorance in war, or competing in a contest—for him they judge at the Delphinion; and if a man in exile, of those for whom there is the possibility of pardon, is charged with killing or wounding someone, for him they judge at Phreatto, and he makes his defence from a boat brought to anchor.

4. These cases the ephetae chosen by lot judge, except those that take place in the Areopagus, and the king introduces them, and they judge in a sanctuary and in the open air, and the king, when he judges, takes off his crown. The man accused is for the rest of the time excluded from the sanctuaries, and the law does not allow him even to enter the Agora; but then he enters the sanctuary and makes his defence. When the killer is not known, the suit is brought against "the doer," and the king and the tribe-kings judge it, and also the cases of inanimate things and the other animals.
1. The polemarch sacrifices to Artemis Agrotera and to Enyalius, and administers the funeral contest, and makes offerings to those who have died in war and to Harmodius and Aristogeiton.

2. Suits are brought before him, the private ones that arise concerning metics and the privileged aliens and the proxenoi; and he must take these and divide them into ten parts and assign to each tribe the part the lot falls on, and those who judge cases for the tribe must hand them over to the arbitrators.

3. He himself introduces suits of desertion of patron and of being without a patron, and of estates and heiresses for metics; and all the other matters that the archon handles for the citizens, the polemarch handles for the metics.

1. The thesmothetae first have authority over the proclaiming of the law-courts, on what days they must sit, then over the assigning of them to the offices; for as these men assign, so do they use them.

2. Further, they bring the impeachments before the people, and they introduce all the votes of condemnation and all the preliminary accusations, and indictments for illegal proposals, and for proposing an unsuitable law, and the cases against presidents and chairmen, and audits of generals.

3. There are also indictments before them for which a deposit is set down: of usurping citizenship, and of bribery to obtain citizenship, if anyone, by giving gifts, escapes a charge of being an alien, and of sycophancy, of bribery, of false entry, of false summons, of conspiracy, of non-registration, and of adultery.
4. They introduce also the scrutinies for all the offices, and the cases of those rejected by the demesmen, and the condemnations from the Council.
5. They introduce also private suits, commercial and mining, and suits of slaves, if anyone speaks ill of a free man. They also allot the law-courts to the offices, both private and public.
6. They ratify also the agreements with foreign cities, and bring in the suits arising from the agreements, and the cases of false witness from the Areopagus.
7. The jurors are allotted by all the nine archons, the tenth being the secretary of the thesmothetae, each allotting those of his own tribe.

1. The matters of the nine archons, then, are of this kind. They allot also ten games-directors, one from each tribe. These, after being scrutinized, hold office for four years, and administer the procession of the Panathenaea and the contest of music and the gymnastic contest and the horse-race, and they have the robe made, and have the amphorae made together with the Council, and give the oil to the athletes.

2. The oil is collected from the sacred olives; the archon exacts it from the owners of the lands in which the sacred olives are, three half-pints from each stump. Formerly the city sold the produce; and if anyone dug up or broke off a sacred olive, the Council of the Areopagus tried him, and if it condemned anyone, they punished him with death. But since the owner of the land pays the oil, the law remains but the trial is abolished. The oil to the city is from the property, not from the stumps.

3. The archon, then, collecting what is produced in his year, hands it over to the treasurers on the Acropolis, and he cannot go up to the Areopagus before he has handed over all to the treasurers. The treasurers keep it on the Acropolis the rest of the time, but at the Panathenaea measure it out to the games-directors, and the games-directors give it to the victorious competitors. For the prizes are, for those who win in music, money and gold objects; for those who win in manly excellence, shields; and for those in the gymnastic contest and the horse-race, oil.

1. They elect by show of hands also all the offices concerned with war: ten generals, formerly one from each tribe, but now from all; and these they arrange by the vote, one over the hoplites, who leads the hoplites if they go out; one over the country, who guards it, and if war arises in the country, this man fights; two over the Piraeus, one for Munichia, one for the Acte, who take charge of the defence and of matters in the Piraeus; one over the symmories, who enrolls the trierarchs and conducts the exchanges of property for them and brings in their adjudications; and the others they send out to deal with present affairs.

2. There is a confirmation-vote on them in each presidency, whether they seem to govern well; and if anyone is rejected by vote, they try him in the law-court, and if he is convicted they assess what he must suffer or pay, but if he is acquitted he holds office again. They have authority, when they are in command, to imprison the disorderly and to dismiss with proclamation and to impose a fine; but they are not in the habit of imposing fines.
3. They elect also ten brigade-commanders, one from each tribe; this man leads his tribesmen and appoints company-commanders.

4. They elect also two cavalry-commanders from all; these lead the cavalry, each dividing the tribes, five each; they have authority over the same matters as the generals over the hoplites. There is a confirmation-vote on these too.
5. They elect also ten tribal commanders, one from each tribe, to lead the cavalry as the brigade-commanders lead the hoplites.
6. They elect also a cavalry-commander for Lemnos, who takes charge of the cavalry in Lemnos.
7. They elect also a treasurer of the Paralus, and now of the Ammon.

1. The allotted offices were formerly some of them allotted from the whole tribe together with the nine archons, and some, allotted in the Theseion, were divided among the demes; but since the demes began to sell the offices, these too are allotted from the whole tribe, except councillors and guards; these they assign to the demes.

2. The people receives pay, first, for the ordinary Assemblies a drachma, but for the principal Assembly nine obols; then the law-courts three obols; then the Council five obols; and to those holding the presidency one obol is added for maintenance. The nine archons receive for maintenance four obols each, and they keep a herald and a flute-player; then the archon for Salamis a drachma a day. The games-directors dine in the Prytaneion in the month Hecatombaion, when the Panathenaea fall, beginning from the fourth of the month. The amphictyons for Delos receive a drachma each day from Delos. And all the offices that are sent out to Samos or Scyros or Lemnos or Imbros receive money for maintenance.
3. It is permitted to hold the offices concerned with war more than once, but none of the others, except to serve in the Council twice.
1. The law-courts the nine archons allot by tribes, and the secretary of the thesmothetae the tenth tribe.

2. There are ten entrances to the law-courts, one for each tribe, and twenty allotment-machines, two for each tribe, and a hundred boxes, ten for each tribe, and other boxes, into which are thrown the tickets of the jurors allotted, and two water-jars. And staves are set out at each entrance, as many as the jurors, and acorns are thrown into the water-jar equal in number to the staves, and on the acorns are inscribed letters of the alphabet from the eleventh, lambda, onward, as many as there are to be law-courts to be filled.

3. It is permitted to serve as juror to those over thirty years of age, all of them who do not owe money to the treasury or are without civic rights. If anyone serves who has no right, information is laid against him and he is brought into the law-court; and if he is convicted, the jurors impose on him in addition whatever he seems worthy to suffer or pay. If he is assessed in money, he must be imprisoned until he pays both the former debt for which he was informed against, and whatever the law-court imposes in addition.

4. Each juror has a boxwood ticket, inscribed with his own name, his father's, and that of his deme, and one letter of the alphabet up to kappa; for the jurors are distributed by tribes into ten parts, nearly equal in each letter.
5. When the thesmothete has allotted the letters that must be assigned to the law-courts, the attendant carries and sets on each law-court the letter allotted to it.

1. The ten boxes lie in front of the entrance for each tribe. On them are inscribed the letters up to kappa. When the jurors throw their tickets into the box on which is inscribed the same letter as is on their ticket, the attendant having shaken it, the thesmothete draws one ticket from each box.

2. This man is called the inserter, and he inserts the tickets from the box into the slot on which the same letter stands as on the box. He is chosen by lot, so that the same man inserting always may not work mischief. There are five slots in each of the allotment-machines.

3. When he has thrown in the dice, the archon allots the tribe by the allotment-machine. The dice are of bronze, black and white. As many jurors as must be allotted, so many white ones are thrown in, one for every five tickets, and the black ones in the same way. When he draws out the dice, the herald calls those allotted. The inserter too is in the number.

4. The man called and answering draws an acorn from the water-jar, and holding it out, showing the letter uppermost, he shows it first to the archon in charge. The archon, when he has seen it, throws his ticket into the box on which is inscribed the same letter as on the acorn, so that he may go into whichever court he is allotted to and not whichever he wishes, and so that it may not be possible to gather into a law-court whatever men one wishes.
5. There stand beside the archon as many boxes as there are to be law-courts to be filled, each having a letter, whichever is that allotted to each law-court.

1. He himself, having shown it again to the attendant, then goes inside the barrier. The attendant gives him a staff of the same colour as the law-court that has the same letter as is on the acorn, so that it shall be necessary for him to enter the law-court he is allotted to; for if he enters another, he is exposed by the colour of the staff.

2. For colours are inscribed on each of the law-courts on the lintel of the entrance. He, taking the staff, goes to the law-court of the same colour as the staff and having the same letter as is on the acorn. When he enters, he receives a token from the public official allotted to this office.
3. Then they who have entered in this way deposit the acorn and the staff in the law-court. To those who fail in the allotment the inserters give back their tickets.

4. The public attendants from each tribe hand over the boxes, one to each law-court, in which are the names of the tribe that are in each of the law-courts. They hand these over to those allotted to give back the tickets to the jurors in each law-court by number, so that from these, calling the men, they may give back the pay.

1. When all the law-courts are full, there are placed in the first of the law-courts two allotment-machines and bronze dice, on which are inscribed the colours of the law-courts, and other dice on which are inscribed the names of the offices. Two of the thesmothetae chosen by lot throw the dice in separately, one the colours into the one allotment-machine, the other the names of the offices into the other. Whichever office is allotted first is proclaimed by the herald to use the first allotted law-court, the second the second, and likewise the others, so that no office may know beforehand which it will use, but each shall use whichever it is allotted.

2. When the jurors have come and been assigned to each court, the official in charge in each law-court draws one ticket from each box, so that there may be ten, one from each tribe, and throws these tickets into another empty box; and of these he allots the first five, one for the water, the other four for the votes, so that no one may pack either the man over the water or those over the votes, and that there may be no mischief about these.

3. The other five who fail in the allotment receive from these men the notice telling where they shall receive their pay and where each tribe shall stand in the law-court itself, when they have judged, so that, separating into groups, they may receive it in small numbers and not, many being crowded into the same place, get in one another's way.

1. Having done these things, they call in the cases: when they try private cases, the private ones, four in number, one from each of the kinds of suit appointed by law, and the litigants swear to speak to the point itself; but when they try public ones, the public, and they try one only.

2. There are water-clocks having little tubes for outflow, into which they pour the water by which the speeches in the suits must be measured. Eleven measures are given for suits over five thousand drachmas, and three for the second speech; seven measures for those up to five thousand, and two; five for those within one thousand, and two; six measures for the adjudications, in which there is no second speech afterward.

3. The man allotted to the water stops up the tube whenever the secretary is about to read out a law or a testimony or some such thing. But when the suit is one for the day measured out, then he does not stop it for him, but equal water is given to the accuser and the defendant.

4. The measuring is done according to the days of the month Posideon . . . they use . . . the jurors . . . into which each . . . for they were eager . . . to thrust out the . . . taking water . . . there are, the one for the prosecutors, the other for the defendants.

5. In the . . . he separated by the vote . . . The day is divided according to the . . . of the suits to which is attached imprisonment or death or exile or loss of civic rights or confiscation of property . . . what one must suffer or pay.

1. Most of the law-courts are of . . . ; but when the public indictments must be brought before one, two law-courts come together in the Heliaea. The . . . into one of fifteen hundred and one, three law-courts.

2. The ballots are of bronze, having a tube in the middle, half of them pierced through, half of them solid. Those allotted to the ballots, when the speeches have been made, give to each of the jurors two ballots, one pierced and one solid, openly to be seen by the litigants, so that no one may take both solid or both pierced. The man allotted to this office takes away the tokens, in return for which each man casting his vote receives a bronze token marked with the figure three (for in giving it back he receives three), so that all may vote; for no one can get the token unless he votes.

3. There are two amphorae set in the law-court, one of bronze, the other of wood, divided so that no one may secretly slip in ballots, into which the jurors cast their votes; the bronze one is the valid one, the wooden the invalid, the bronze one having a lid pierced so that only the ballot itself can pass through, that the same man may not throw in two.

4. When the jurors are about to vote, the herald proclaims first, if the litigants object to the testimonies; for it is not possible to object once they have begun to vote. Then again he proclaims: "The pierced ballot for the one who spoke first, the solid for the one who spoke last." The juror, taking the ballots from the stand, pressing the tube of the ballot and not showing the litigants either the pierced or the solid, casts the valid one into the bronze amphora, the invalid into the wooden.

1. When all have voted, the attendants take the valid amphora and empty it onto a board having as many holes as there are ballots, so that these may lie out clearly and be easily counted, and the pierced and the solid be plain to the litigants. Those allotted to the ballots count them on the board, the solid separately, the pierced separately. And the herald proclaims the number of the ballots, the pierced for the prosecutor, the solid for the defendant; and whichever has the more, this man wins, but if they are equal, the defendant.

2. Then again they assess, if assessment is needed, voting in the same way, giving back the token and taking again a staff. The assessment is by half a measure of water for each side. When the matters required by the laws have been adjudged for them, they receive their pay in the portion allotted to each.

1. Epitome of Heraclides 1: (From the work of Heraclides on the Constitutions.)
The Athenians at first used kingship. When Ion settled among them, then for the first time they were called Ionians. Pandion, having reigned after Erechtheus, divided the rule among his sons; and these continued at strife with one another.

2. Harpocration:
Apollo Patroös, the Pythian. This is a title of the god, there being many others. The Athenians honour Apollo in common as Patroös, from Ion; for when this man settled in Attica, as Aristotle says, the Athenians were called Ionians, and Apollo was named Patroös to them.

3. Scholiast on Aristophanes, Birds 1537:
The Athenians honour Apollo as Patroös, since Ion the polemarch of the Athenians was born of Apollo and Creusa, the wife of Xuthus.
Cf. Bekker, Anecdota 291 = Scholiast on Plato, Euthydemus 302 C.

1. Plutarch, Theseus 25:
Wishing still further to increase the city, Theseus invited all on equal terms, and the proclamation "Come hither, all you peoples" is said to have been Theseus's, when he was establishing a kind of commonwealth of all. Yet he did not allow the democracy to become disordered or confused by an indiscriminate multitude pouring in; rather he was the first to set apart separately the eupatrids and the farmers and the craftsmen, and assigning to the eupatrids the knowledge of divine things and the providing of the magistrates and the being teachers of the laws and expounders of sacred and holy things, he established the other citizens, as it were, on an equal footing—the eupatrids being thought to excel in reputation, the farmers in usefulness, the craftsmen in number. That he was the first to incline toward the masses, as Aristotle says, and gave up sole rule, Homer too seems to bear witness, in the catalogue of ships naming the Athenians alone "the people."

1. Scholiast on Plato, Axiochus 371 D (cf. Moeris, Atticist p. 193. 16) on the word "clansman":
Aristotle says that, the whole multitude at Athens being divided into farmers and craftsmen, their tribes were four, and of each of the tribes there were three parts, which they call thirds and brotherhoods, and of each of these there were thirty clans, and each clan was composed of thirty men. These men, then, who were arranged into the clans, they call clansmen.

2. Patmos Lexicon p. 152 Sakkelion, on "clansman":
In old times the multitude of the Athenians, before Cleisthenes arranged the matters concerning the tribes, was divided into farmers and craftsmen. And their tribes were four, and each of the tribes had three parts, which they called brotherhoods and thirds. And each of these was composed of thirty clans, and each clan had thirty men, those arranged into the clans, who were called clansmen, from whom the priesthoods belonging to each were allotted—for instance the Eumolpidae and the Heralds and the Eteobutadae—as Aristotle records in the Constitution of the Athenians, saying thus: "Their tribes were divided into four, in imitation of the seasons in the year, and each of the tribes was divided into three parts, so that there might be twelve parts in all, just as the months in the year, and they were called thirds and brotherhoods; and into the brotherhood thirty clans were arranged, just as the days into the month, and the clan was of thirty men."

3. Harpocration, on "third":
A third is the third part of the tribe; for this is divided into three parts, thirds and races and brotherhoods, as Aristotle says in the Constitution of the Athenians.
